disclaimer: General information only, not medical advice. In an emergency call 112.

call_112_when: Bleeding does not stop after 10 minutes of firm pressure
Blood is spurting from the wound
The person faints or becomes unresponsive
The wound was caused by a serious accident
danger_signs: Bleeding that does not stop after 10 minutes of pressure
Pale, cold or clammy skin, dizziness or fainting
guides.disclaimer: General information only, not medical advice. In an emergency call 112.
steps: Call 112 if the bleeding is heavy or will not stop.
Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or bandage.
Keep pressing without lifting the cloth to check. If blood soaks through, add another cloth on top.
Raise the injured part above the level of the heart if possible.
Keep the person still and warm until help arrives.
guides.title: Severe Bleeding
what_not_to_do: Do not remove an object stuck in the wound.
Do not stop pressing to look at the wound.
Do not give food or drink.

call_112_when: The burn is large or deep
The burn is on the face, hands, feet or groin
The person has difficulty breathing
A child or older person has a significant burn
danger_signs: Burn larger than the person's palm
Burn on the face, hands, feet or groin
Skin that looks white, charred or deep
Burn caused by chemicals or electricity
guides.disclaimer: General information only, not medical advice. In an emergency call 112.
steps: Cool the burn with clean, cool running water for at least 10 minutes.
Remove jewellery or loose clothing near the burn, unless it is stuck to the skin.
Cover the burn loosely with clean cling film or a clean cloth.
Keep the person warm and comfortable.
guides.title: Burns
what_not_to_do: Do not use ice, butter, toothpaste or creams on a burn.
Do not pop blisters.
Do not peel off clothing stuck to the burn.

call_112_when: The person cannot breathe, cough or speak
Lips or face turn blue
The person becomes unresponsive
guides.disclaimer: General information only, not medical advice. In an emergency call 112.
steps: If the person can cough, encourage them to keep coughing.
Give up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
If that does not work, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts: stand behind, clasp hands above the navel and pull sharply inwards and upwards.
Repeat back blows and abdominal thrusts until the object comes out.
If the person becomes unresponsive, call 112 and start CPR.
guides.title: Choking (Adult)
what_not_to_do: Do not sweep your fingers inside the mouth unless you can clearly see the object.
Do not give water or food.

call_112_when: The child cannot cry, cough or breathe
Lips turn blue
The child becomes unresponsive
guides.disclaimer: General information only, not medical advice. In an emergency call 112.
steps: For an infant under 1 year: hold the baby face down along your forearm with the head lower than the chest. Give up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades, then turn the baby over and give up to 5 chest thrusts with two fingers on the centre of the chest.
For a child over 1 year: give up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts, gentler than for an adult.
Repeat until the object comes out.
If the child becomes unresponsive, call 112 and start CPR.
guides.title: Choking (Child / Infant)
what_not_to_do: Do not shake the baby.
Do not sweep your fingers inside the mouth unless you can clearly see the object.
Do not give food or drink.

call_112_when: Always. Call 112 immediately if someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
danger_signs: Not breathing normally (no breathing, or only occasional gasps)
guides.disclaimer: General information only, not medical advice. In an emergency call 112.
steps: Check for a response by tapping the shoulders and shouting.
Call 112 immediately, or ask someone else to call.
Place the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest, the other hand on top.
Push hard and fast, about 100 to 120 compressions per minute, letting the chest rise between pushes.
Give 30 compressions, then 2 rescue breaths if you are trained to do so.
Keep going until help arrives or the person starts breathing normally.
guides.title: CPR Basics
what_not_to_do: Do not stop unless you are exhausted or help takes over.
Do not move the person unless they are in danger.
Do not give food or drink.

call_112_when: A bone is visible through the skin
There is heavy bleeding with the fracture
The head, neck or spine may be injured
The person is unresponsive
danger_signs: Cannot move or use the limb
guides.disclaimer: General information only, not medical advice. In an emergency call 112.
steps: Keep the injured limb still and supported with padding or a sling.
Apply a cold pack wrapped in a cloth to reduce swelling.
Do not move the person more than necessary.
Call 112 if the injury is severe or a bone is visible.
guides.title: Fracture (Broken Bone)
what_not_to_do: Do not try to straighten the limb.
Do not press on a bone sticking out.
Do not give food or drink, as an operation may be needed.

call_112_when: The limb looks deformed
There is numbness in the limb
The injury followed a serious fall or accident
danger_signs: Pain, swelling and bruising around a joint
Cannot bear weight on the limb
Joint looks deformed or feels numb
guides.disclaimer: General information only, not medical advice. In an emergency call 112.
steps: Rest the injured joint and avoid using it.
Apply a cold pack wrapped in a cloth for 15 to 20 minutes.
Apply a bandage snugly, but not so tight that it cuts off circulation.
Raise the limb above the level of the heart.
guides.title: Sprain
what_not_to_do: Do not apply heat in the first two days.
Do not massage the injured area.
Do not walk on an injured ankle or foot.

call_112_when: Always. Call 112 for every snake bite, even if the person feels fine at first.
danger_signs: Pain and swelling spreading from the bite
guides.disclaimer: General information only, not medical advice. In an emergency call 112.
steps: Call 112 straight away for any snake bite.
Keep the person calm and still. Movement spreads venom faster.
Keep the bitten limb still and below the level of the heart.
Remove rings, watches or tight clothing near the bite.
Note the time of the bite and, only if it is safe, what the snake looked like.
guides.title: Snake Bite
what_not_to_do: Do not suck out the venom or cut the wound.
Do not tie a tight band around the limb.
Do not apply ice.
Do not try to catch or kill the snake.

call_112_when: They do not wake up within a minute
They have chest pain or difficulty breathing
They were injured in the fall
They fainted during exercise
Fainting happens again and again
guides.disclaimer: General information only, not medical advice. In an emergency call 112.
steps: Lay the person flat on their back.
Raise their legs slightly to help blood flow to the brain.
Loosen tight clothing and let in fresh air.
When they wake up, keep them lying down for a few minutes, then help them sit up slowly.
Give small sips of water once fully awake.
guides.title: Fainting
what_not_to_do: Do not crowd around the person.
Do not slap or shake them.
Do not give food or drink while they are unconscious.
Do not stand them up quickly.

call_112_when: The person is confused, fits, or unresponsive
Body temperature is very high
Cooling does not help quickly
danger_signs: Very hot skin, with heavy sweating or no sweating at all
guides.disclaimer: General information only, not medical advice. In an emergency call 112.
steps: Call 112 straight away if the person is confused or unresponsive.
Move the person to a cool, shaded place.
Remove extra clothing and cool the skin with wet cloths and a fan.
If the person is fully awake, give small sips of cool water.
guides.title: Heatstroke
what_not_to_do: Do not give alcohol or caffeinated drinks.
Do not put the person in an ice-cold bath.
Do not leave them alone.

call_112_when: Always. Call 112 immediately for any sign of a severe allergic reaction.
danger_signs: Swelling of the face, lips or tongue
guides.disclaimer: General information only, not medical advice. In an emergency call 112.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Do not wait to see if it gets better.
Help the person use their allergy auto-injector if they carry one.
Lay the person flat with legs raised. If they are struggling to breathe or vomiting, lay them on their side.
Stay with them until help arrives.
If there is no improvement after 5 minutes and a second auto-injector is available, help them use it.
guides.title: Severe Allergic Reaction (Anaphylaxis)
what_not_to_do: Do not wait and watch.
Do not give food or drink.
Do not stand the person up or make them walk.

call_112_when: Bleeding lasts more than 20 minutes
Bleeding is very heavy
The nosebleed followed a serious head injury
The person feels faint
danger_signs: Bleeding from one or both nostrils
guides.disclaimer: General information only, not medical advice. In an emergency call 112.
steps: Sit upright and lean slightly forward.
Pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10 to 15 minutes without letting go.
Breathe through the mouth.
Place a cold cloth on the bridge of the nose.
guides.title: Nosebleed
what_not_to_do: Do not tilt the head back.
Do not blow the nose.
Do not pick the nose or push cotton deep inside.

call_112_when: The seizure lasts more than 5 minutes
Seizures repeat without the person waking up
The person has trouble breathing afterwards
They were injured during the seizure
It is their first ever seizure
danger_signs: Foaming at the mouth or loss of bladder control
guides.disclaimer: General information only, not medical advice. In an emergency call 112.
steps: Stay calm and note the time the seizure starts.
Clear away hard or sharp objects nearby.
Cushion the head with something soft.
Once the jerking stops, gently turn the person on their side.
Stay with them until they are fully awake and explain what happened.
guides.title: Seizure (Fit)
what_not_to_do: Do not hold the person down.
Do not put anything in their mouth.
Do not give food or drink until they are fully awake.
